questions.mark_scheme:
M1 for identifying that $AC$ is a diameter and correctly stating the circle theorem (the angle in a semicircle is $90^\circ$) as the reason.
A1 for $x = 90^\circ$ with correct reason stated (e.g. "angle in a semicircle is $90^\circ$").
Note: No marks awarded if student treats $AC$ as a chord rather than the diameter, or gives reason based on an incorrect theorem.

questions.topic_aspect: Angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference
questions.mark_scheme:
M1 for using the circle theorem "angle at centre = twice angle at circumference" and correctly setting up $x = 136 \div 2$ (or equivalent, e.g. $2x = 136$)
A1 for $x = 68^\circ$ (award A0 if $x = 272^\circ$ from doubling instead of halving)
questions.misconception_targeted: Halving instead of doubling, or applying theorem to angles not subtending same arc

questions.topic_aspect: Angles in the same segment are equal
questions.mark_scheme:
M1 for identifying that angle ACD and angle ABD are both subtended by (stand on) the same arc/chord AD, from the same side of the chord
M1 for correctly stating that angle ACD = angle ABD (angles in the same segment are equal), independent of the 24° figure which is not required for this part
A1 for angle ACD = 38° with reason "angles in the same segment (subtended by the same arc AD) are equal" stated
Note: the 24° (angle BDC) is a distractor angle not required to find ACD; full marks require correct identification that ACD and ABD subtend the same arc AD, not BC or another chord
questions.misconception_targeted: Not identifying which arc/segment the angles subtend

questions.topic_aspect: Cyclic quadrilaterals — opposite angles sum to 180°
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) M1 for forming the correct equation: (2x+10) + (3x-5) = 180 (using the property that opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°); A1 for x = 35 (correctly solving 5x + 5 = 180)
(b) M1 for substituting x = 35 into both expressions: 2(35)+10 = 80 and 3(35)-5 = 100; A1 for correct angles DAB = 80° and DCB = 100°, with reason stated: "opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°" (accept "sum to 180° as ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral")
Total: 4 marks
questions.misconception_targeted: Assuming all opposite angles are equal rather than supplementary

questions.topic_aspect: Tangent to a circle — perpendicular to radius, and two tangents from an external point
questions.mark_scheme:
M1 for identifying that angle OAP = 90 degrees and angle OBP = 90 degrees (tangent perpendicular to radius)
M1 for using angle sum of quadrilateral OAPB = 360 degrees (or splitting into two right-angled triangles using the isosceles triangle OAB and tangent lengths PA = PB)
M1 for correct method: 360 - 90 - 90 - 46 = 134
A1 for angle AOB = 134 degrees (accept answer with correct units/degree symbol)

questions.correct_answer: Angle TAB = 71 degrees (shown using the alternate segment theorem)
questions.mark_scheme:
M1 for identifying that angle PTB is the angle between the tangent PT and the chord TB (given as 71 degrees)
M1 for correctly identifying that angle TAB is the angle in the alternate segment to angle PTB (i.e. angle TAB is subtended by chord TB from the opposite/alternate side of the circle to where the tangent-chord angle is measured, NOT the angle on the same side as the tangent angle)
A1 for correctly quoting the alternate segment theorem: "the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment"
A1 (dependent on above) for concluding angle TAB = angle PTB = 71 degrees, therefore x = 71 degrees, with clear reasoning stated (e.g. "by the alternate segment theorem, angle TAB = angle between tangent PT and chord TB = 71 degrees")

Note: Award 0 for M1 (second) if student states angle TAB equals the angle in the adjacent segment (i.e. confuses with angle ATB or similar) without correct identification of the alternate segment.
questions.misconception_targeted: Confusing the alternate segment angle with the angle in the adjacent segment

questions.topic_aspect: Combined circle theorems (multi-step reasoning) in an applied science context
questions.correct_answer: (a) Angle POR = 284 degrees (reflex); (b) Angle PSR = 76 degrees; (c) Angle PRS = 42 degrees
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) M1 for using angle at centre = 2 x angle at circumference (angle PQR is on major arc, so reflex angle POR = 2 x 142); A1 for angle POR = 284 degrees, with reason "angle at centre is twice angle at circumference" stated.

(b) M1 for using cyclic quadrilateral property: angle PQR + angle PSR = 180 (opposite angles of cyclic quadrilateral PQRS sum to 180); A1 for angle PSR = 180 - 142 = 38... 

[Note: corrected calculation - see below]

M1 for recognising PQRS is a cyclic quadrilateral and opposite angles sum to 180 degrees, with reason stated; A1 for angle PSR = 180 - 142 = 38 degrees.

(c) M1 for using angle sum of triangle PSR (angles QPS, PSR known contribute to triangle PQS or similar) combined with reason to find angle PRS: using triangle PSR, angle SPR = angle QPS - angle QPR (from part working), and angle sum of triangle = 180, leading to angle PRS = 180 - angle PSR - angle SPR; A1 for correct final value with reasons clearly stated (angles in a triangle sum to 180 degrees, and angle SRO = 34 degrees used to isolate angle ORS from angle PRS if required).

Full marks require reasons quoted at each stage (angle at centre = 2x angle at circumference; opposite angles in cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180 degrees; angles in a triangle sum to 180 degrees) - 1 mark deducted per part if reason omitted despite correct numerical answer.
questions.misconception_targeted: Applying only one theorem when a chain of reasoning across multiple theorems is required
